\chapter{The Compound Past}
\label{ch:passe-compose}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build and use French's everyday past tense, and recognise the second past tense that only appears in writing.}

French's everyday past is avoir plus a participle that never moves, so it costs one new form rather than six. It exists because habeō litterās scriptās once meant plain possession — 'I have letters, written ones' — and hardened into a tense, which is also why a participle still agrees when its object comes first. Then the other past: il parla, which you read in every novel and never hear. It is the same inherited tense Spanish says every day as habló, and it retreated into writing across a connected block of France, southern Germany and northern Italy while the languages at the western edge kept theirs.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[parlé]{parlé — the past participle}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-participe-er}



\begin{quote}
Before French can talk about the past it needs one new form of the verb, and for the verbs you already have it is the smallest change imaginable.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -er becomes -é}]
Take an \textbf{-er} verb and put an accent where the \textbf{r} was:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{parler} $\to$ \textbf{parlé} · \textbf{habiter} $\to$ \textbf{habité} · \textbf{travailler} $\to$ \textbf{travaillé}
\end{quote}

That form is the \textbf{past participle}. On its own it is not a tense and not even really a verb — it is closer to an adjective, and \emph{parlé} means something like \textquotedblleft{}spoken,\textquotedblright{} the way \emph{written} or \emph{broken} work in English.

That is worth holding on to, because it explains everything this chapter does next. You are not learning a past tense yet. You are learning a \textbf{part}, and the tense gets built out of it in the next lesson.

All three of your \textbf{-er} verbs behave identically. There is no list to learn and no exception in this class at all.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the swap — \textquotedblleft{}parler, parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the other two — \textquotedblleft{}habiter, habité; travailler, travaillé\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it is — \textquotedblleft{}spoken, lived, worked: adjectives, not tenses\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the past participle of \emph{parler}? (\textbf{parlé}.) What changes? (The \textbf{-er} becomes \textbf{-é}.) Is \emph{parlé} a past tense on its own? (\textbf{No} — it is closer to an \textbf{adjective}, \textquotedblleft{}spoken.\textquotedblright{}) Give the participles of \emph{habiter} and \emph{travailler}. (\textbf{habité}, \textbf{travaillé}.) Next: what to build with it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[j'ai parlé]{j'ai parlé — the past built from \textquotedblleft{}have\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-jai-parle}



\begin{quote}
You have both halves of French's everyday past tense already. This lesson only puts them next to each other.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: avoir, then the participle}]
The recipe is two words:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{avoir} (conjugated) \textbf{+ past participle}
\end{quote}

So, with \emph{parlé}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{j'ai parlé} — I spoke, I have spoken
  \item \textbf{tu as parlé} — you spoke
  \item \textbf{il a parlé} — he spoke
  \item \textbf{nous avons parlé} — we spoke
  \item \textbf{ils ont parlé} — they spoke
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Only \emph{avoir} changes.} The participle sits there, identical in every line. So this is not six new forms — it is the verb you spent last chapter on, with one unchanging word after it.

Notice too that French makes no distinction English insists on. \emph{J'ai parlé} is both \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I have spoken\textquotedblright{}; there is no separate form for the two. Where English has two past tenses to choose between, French conversation mostly has this one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the recipe — \textquotedblleft{}avoir, then the participle\textquotedblright{}
  \item the run — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, tu as parlé, il a parlé, nous avons parlé, ils ont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item another verb — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai travaillé, j'ai habité\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two English meanings — \textquotedblleft{}I spoke, I have spoken; French has one form\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, tu as parlé, il a parlé\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two parts of the compound past? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}} \textbf{conjugated}, then the \textbf{past participle}.) Which part changes with the person? (\textbf{Only \emph{avoir}.}) Say \textquotedblleft{}we worked.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Nous avons travaillé}.) How many English tenses does \emph{j'ai parlé} cover? (\textbf{Two} — \textquotedblleft{}I spoke\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I have spoken\textquotedblright{}.) Next: a spelling trap you cannot hear.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parler · parlé · parlez]{parler · parlé · parlez — one sound, three jobs}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-parler-parle-parlez}



\begin{quote}
Say the infinitive, the participle and the \emph{vous} form out loud, one after the other. Now try to hear a difference.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: your ear gets no help at all}]
\textbf{parler}, \textbf{parlé} and \textbf{parlez} are pronounced \textbf{exactly the same}: \emph{par-LAY}.

Three different jobs, three different spellings, one sound:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parler} — to speak (the infinitive)
  \item \textbf{parlé} — spoken (the participle)
  \item \textbf{parlez} — you speak (the \emph{vous} form)
\end{itemize}

This is the same phenomenon you met with \emph{ai}, \emph{as} and \emph{a}, and it has the same cause: French endings survive on the page and die in the mouth. But it lands harder here, because these three are \textbf{different parts of speech}, and only the sentence around them says which one you heard.

The good news is that the sentence always does. \emph{Vous parlez} has a pronoun in front of it. \emph{J'ai parlé} has \emph{avoir} in front of it. \textbf{Parler} has nothing in front of it, or a verb like \emph{vouloir}. In practice you never have to decide — which is why French speakers are untroubled by a distinction that looks impossible written down.

For \textbf{writing}, though, you do have to choose, and choosing wrongly is the single most common spelling mistake native French speakers make.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three — \textquotedblleft{}parler, parlé, parlez\textquotedblright{}; one sound
  \item each in its frame — \textquotedblleft{}vous parlez\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule of thumb — \textquotedblleft{}what comes before it tells you which\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many of \emph{parler}, \emph{parlé} and \emph{parlez} sound different? (\textbf{None} — all three are \emph{par-LAY}.) What tells you which one you are hearing? (\textbf{What comes before it} — a pronoun, \emph{avoir}, or nothing.) Which is the participle? (\textbf{parlé}.) Next: the verbs that do not end in \emph{-er}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[fini · vendu]{fini · vendu — the other two classes}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-participe-ir-re}



\begin{quote}
Every verb you have met so far ends in \textbf{-er}. That is by far the biggest group, and it is not the only one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three classes, three vowels}]
French verbs are sorted by how the infinitive ends, and each group makes its participle with its own vowel:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{infinitive ends in} & \textbf{participle ends in} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-er} & \textbf{-é} & \emph{parler} $\to$ \emph{parlé} \\
\textbf{-ir} & \textbf{-i} & \emph{finir} $\to$ \emph{fini} \\
\textbf{-re} & \textbf{-u} & \emph{vendre} $\to$ \emph{vendu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{finir} (\textquotedblleft{}to finish\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{vendre} (\textquotedblleft{}to sell\textquotedblright{}) are the standard examples, and they are here as \textbf{examples of the pattern} rather than words to add to your vocabulary — neither has appeared in this book yet. What you want from this lesson is the shape: when you meet a verb, its infinitive ending already tells you what its participle will look like.

That is three facts, not three hundred. And \textbf{-er} is the group that matters most in practice: it holds the overwhelming majority of French verbs, and it is the only group still taking new members — every verb French invents or borrows becomes an \emph{-er} verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three endings — \textquotedblleft{}é, i, u\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three pairs — \textquotedblleft{}parler parlé, finir fini, vendre vendu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the useful half — \textquotedblleft{}-er is the big one, and the only one still growing\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What vowel ends the participle of an \textbf{-ir} verb? (\textbf{-i}.) And an \textbf{-re} verb? (\textbf{-u}.) And \textbf{-er}? (\textbf{-é}.) Which class is by far the largest? (\textbf{-er} — and it is the only one that still takes new verbs.) Next: where those three endings came from.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[-ātum · -ītum · -ūtum]{-ātum · -ītum · -ūtum — where the endings came from}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-participe-latin}



\begin{quote}
Three participle vowels, and two of them are inherited. The third is French tidying up after itself, which is a different kind of fact.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin marked its participles with a \textbf{-t-} and a vowel in front of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{parlé} $\leftarrow$ \emph{-ātum}
  \item \textbf{fini} $\leftarrow$ \emph{-ītum}
  \item \textbf{vendu} $\leftarrow$ \emph{-ūtum}
\end{itemize}

French wore away the \textbf{-t-} and the ending, and kept the vowel. English, which borrowed from Latin rather than inheriting it, kept the \textbf{-t-} instead — you can see it whole in \textbf{fini\emph{te}}, \textbf{acu\emph{te}}, \textbf{statu\emph{te}}. Same suffix, two salvage strategies: French saved the vowel, English saved the consonant.

Now the third one, which is the interesting one. \emph{\textbf{-ūtus\emph{ was rare in Latin.\textbf{ It turns up in a handful of words — \emph{minūtus} (small, hence \emph{minute}), \emph{tribūtus} (assigned, hence \emph{tribute}) — and nothing like a whole class.}}}}

French and Italian took that small, scrappy group and \textbf{spread it across an entire conjugation}. So \emph{-é} and \emph{-i} are straight inheritance, and \emph{-u} is largely the language \textbf{tidying up by analogy}: a pattern noticed in a few words and then applied on purpose to many.

That is worth separating from ordinary etymology. Most of what this book shows you is erosion — words wearing down. This is the opposite force: speakers \textbf{regularising}, making a language tidier than they received it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three Latin endings — \textquotedblleft{}-ātum, -ītum, -ūtum\textquotedblright{}
  \item what English kept — \textquotedblleft{}finite, acute, statute\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{t} survived
  \item the odd one — \textquotedblleft{}-ūtus was rare, and French spread it\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two forces — \textquotedblleft{}erosion wears words down; analogy tidies them up\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did French keep from the Latin participle ending, and what did English keep? (French kept the \textbf{vowel}; English kept the \textbf{-t-}, as in \emph{finite}, \emph{acute}, \emph{statute}.) Which of the three French endings is \textbf{not} straight inheritance? (\textbf{-u} — \emph{-ūtus} was \textbf{rare} in Latin and French spread it over a whole class.) What is that process called? (\textbf{Analogy} — speakers regularising.) Next: why this tense exists at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[habeō litterās scriptās]{habeō litterās scriptās — the buried possessive}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-possessif}



\begin{quote}
There is an obvious question about this tense that is worth asking: why \emph{have}? What does owning something have to do with the past?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it was never a tense to begin with}]
Latin could say:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{habeō litterās scriptās} — \textquotedblleft{}I \emph{have} letters, written ones.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Read that as Latin, not as French. It is \textbf{not} a past tense. It is \emph{habēre} in its plain, ordinary sense — \textbf{I possess some letters} — with \emph{scriptās} as an \textbf{adjective} describing them, agreeing with \emph{litterās} in gender and number the way any Latin adjective would.

The sentence says nothing about who did the writing, and nothing about when. It says: I own letters, and their condition is \emph{written}.

Then centuries pass. The phrase gets said constantly, the possession fades out of it, and what is left is the doing: \emph{I wrote}. A construction about \textbf{owning} an object hardened into a construction about \textbf{having done} an action.

This happens to be one of the best-documented examples of the whole process, and you can watch it happen in the surviving texts. It is also why English \textquotedblleft{}I have written\textquotedblright{} exists — English built the same thing, from the same starting point, independently.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the Latin — \textquotedblleft{}habeō litterās scriptās\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it meant — \textquotedblleft{}I have letters, written ones\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it became — \textquotedblleft{}I wrote\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shift in one line — \textquotedblleft{}possession hardened into a tense\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{habeō litterās scriptās} originally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I have letters, written ones}\textquotedblright{} — plain possession.) What part of speech was \emph{scriptās}? (An \textbf{adjective}, describing the letters.) What did the phrase turn into? (A \textbf{past tense} — \textquotedblleft{}I wrote\textquotedblright{}.) Why does French build its past out of \emph{have}? (Because the construction \textbf{began} as one about \textbf{having}.) Next: the fossil that construction left behind.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[les lettres que j'ai écrites]{les lettres que j'ai écrites — the fossil}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-accord}



\begin{quote}
The possessive is gone from the meaning. It is not gone from the spelling, and the place it survives is one of the strangest rules in French.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the participle still agrees, when the object goes first}]
Normally the participle never changes:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{J'ai écrit les lettres.} — \textquotedblleft{}I wrote the letters.\textquotedblright{} \emph{écrit}, plain.
\end{quote}

Move the object in front of the verb, though, and the participle \textbf{agrees with it} — feminine, plural, exactly as an adjective would:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Les lettres que j'ai écrites.} — \textquotedblleft{}The letters that I wrote.\textquotedblright{} \emph{écrit\textbf{es}}.
\end{quote}

That \textbf{-es} is the two-thousand-year-old adjective ending from \emph{habeō litterās scriptās}, still doing the job it was doing in Latin. The meaning moved on; the agreement stayed behind.

Two things make this bearable. First, you can almost never \textbf{hear} it — \emph{écrit} and \emph{écrites} sound the same, so it is a writing rule far more than a speaking one. Second, it now has an explanation instead of being arbitrary: the participle agrees when the thing it describes comes \textbf{before} it, which is where an adjective could still see it.

French schoolchildren spend years on this rule and are taught it as a list of conditions. It is really one fact with a very long memory.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the plain order — \textquotedblleft{}J'ai écrit les lettres\textquotedblright{}
  \item the object first — \textquotedblleft{}Les lettres que j'ai écrites\textquotedblright{}
  \item what the \emph{-es} is — \textquotedblleft{}an adjective ending, two thousand years old\textquotedblright{}
  \item the consolation — \textquotedblleft{}you cannot hear it\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does the past participle agree with the object? (When the object comes \textbf{before} the verb.) Why does it agree at all? (Because it was an \textbf{adjective} first, describing the thing that was possessed.) Can you hear the agreement in \emph{écrites}? (\textbf{No} — it is a writing rule.) Next: all of it, together.
\end{tcolorbox}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-practice-compose}

  \item with your other verbs — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai travaillé, nous avons habité\textquotedblright{}

\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, tu as parlé, il a parlé\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: the three endings}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}é, i, u\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pairs — \textquotedblleft{}parler parlé, finir fini, vendre vendu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin — \textquotedblleft{}-ātum, -ītum, -ūtum\textquotedblright{}; and English \textquotedblleft{}finite, acute, statute\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}

  \item the old meaning — \textquotedblleft{}I have letters, written ones\textquotedblright{}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a past tense}, made of a verb you already knew and one unchanging word.
  \item \textbf{three participle endings}, one per verb class, two inherited and one spread by analogy.
  \item \textbf{an explanation for the \emph{have}}: the construction began as plain possession — \emph{I have letters, written ones} — and hardened into a tense.
  \item \textbf{a fossil you can point at}: the agreement in \emph{écrites} is an adjective ending that has outlived the grammar that required it.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}we spoke.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Nous avons parlé}.) Which half changes with the person? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}}.) Give the three participle vowels. (\textbf{-é, -i, -u}.) Which three forms of \emph{parler} sound identical? (\emph{\textbf{parler, parlé, parlez}}.) When does the participle agree? (When the \textbf{object comes first}.) Next: the other past tense — the one you will read and never say.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il parla]{il parla — the past you read but never say}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-passe-simple}



\begin{quote}
French has a \textbf{second} past tense. You will meet it on the first page of almost any novel and never once hear it in a conversation.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: recognise it, do not produce it}]
It is called the \textbf{passé simple}, and it is one word where the compound past is two:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{meaning} & \textbf{passé simple} & \textbf{passé composé} \\
\midrule
he spoke & \emph{il parla} & \emph{il a parlé} \\
they spoke & \emph{ils parlèrent} & \emph{ils ont parlé} \\
he had & \emph{il eut} & \emph{il a eu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You do \textbf{not} need to produce these, and you should not try. Nobody says them. Using one out loud sounds roughly like announcing \textquotedblleft{}thus spake he\textquotedblright{} in an English café.

What you need is to \textbf{recognise} them, because they carry the past tense of essentially all French literature. A reader who stalls at \emph{il parla} stalls on page one of everything.

So this is the first thing in this book that is deliberately \textbf{half}-learned, and that is a real distinction worth making: some things you learn to say, and some you learn only to understand. Treating those as the same job is what makes beginners feel they must master everything before reading anything.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}il parla … il a parlé\textquotedblright{}; same meaning, two registers
  \item the plural pair — \textquotedblleft{}ils parlèrent … ils ont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item where you meet it — \textquotedblleft{}in a novel, not a conversation\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{il parla}? (The \textbf{passé simple} — \textquotedblleft{}he spoke\textquotedblright{}.) Where will you meet it? (In \textbf{writing}, especially novels — never in speech.) Do you need to produce it? (\textbf{No} — recognition only.) What is the everyday equivalent? (\emph{\textbf{il a parlé}}.) Next: who else kept this tense alive.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il parla · habló · falou]{il parla · habló · falou — the same tense, four fates}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-soeurs}



\begin{quote}
The tense French retired to its libraries is a tense other people use to order coffee.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{il parla} comes from the plain Latin perfect, handed straight down with no rebuilding at all. Which means it is the \textbf{same tense} as these:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}he spoke\textquotedblright{}} & \textbf{status} \\
\midrule
French & \emph{il parla} & books only \\
Spanish & \emph{habló} & everyday speech \\
Portuguese & \emph{falou} & everyday speech \\
Italian & \emph{parlò} & regional \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

One Latin ancestor, four different fates. A Spaniard saying \emph{habló} and a French novelist writing \emph{il parla} are using the \textbf{same inherited form}, and only one of them sounds archaic doing it.

That is worth sitting with, because it undoes an assumption. A tense is not formal or informal, literary or everyday, by its nature. \textbf{Register is not a property of a form; it is a property of what a particular community of speakers happens to have kept.} French did not decide \emph{il parla} was fancy. It just stopped saying it, and the books did not.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the sisters — \textquotedblleft{}il parla, habló, falou, parlò\textquotedblright{}
  \item the split — \textquotedblleft{}one of them is literary; the others are lunch\textquotedblright{}
  \item the finding — \textquotedblleft{}register is not in the form, it is in the speakers\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What Latin tense is \emph{il parla}? (The plain \textbf{perfect}, inherited directly.) Which languages still say it every day? (\textbf{Spanish} — \emph{habló} — and \textbf{Portuguese} — \emph{falou}.) So what makes a tense \textquotedblleft{}literary\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Not the form} — what its speakers kept using.) Next: what pushed it out, and where else that happened.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[passé simple · Präteritum · passato …]{the same retreat, three times over}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-areal}



\begin{quote}
French pushed its old past tense into books and replaced it with a compound built on \emph{have}. It is not the only language that did.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{the simple past} & \textbf{what replaced it in speech} \\
\midrule
French & \emph{passé simple} & \emph{passé composé} — \emph{j'ai parlé} \\
German & \emph{Präteritum} & \emph{Perfekt} — \emph{ich habe gesagt} \\
Italian & \emph{passato remoto} & \emph{passato prossimo} — \emph{ho parlato} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three languages, two Romance and one \textbf{Germanic}, each built a compound past out of \textquotedblleft{}have,\textquotedblright{} and each let that compound push the inherited simple past out of conversation and into writing.

The obvious reading is that this is a natural drift any language might undergo. The better reading is geographical. \textbf{France, southern Germany and northern Italy form one connected block}, and the change spread through it by \textbf{contact}, over the same few centuries — carried by people who lived near each other, across language boundaries that were never barriers to anything.

Linguists call that an \textbf{areal} change: one that travels by neighbourhood rather than by descent. And the evidence is at the edges. \textbf{Spanish and Portuguese}, out at the western rim, largely \textbf{did not get it} — they kept their simple past in everyday speech, which is why \emph{habló} is still ordinary. Though Spain's Spanish has begun drifting the same way, with \emph{he hablado} taking ground: the change reaching the edge, late.

So the map explains what the family tree cannot. Italian and Spanish are close relatives that behave differently here, and French and German are distant relatives that behave the same — because what mattered was who was standing next to whom.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three retreats — \textquotedblleft{}passé simple, Präteritum, passato remoto\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three replacements — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, ich habe gesagt, ho parlato\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shape — \textquotedblleft{}a connected block: France, southern Germany, northern Italy\textquotedblright{}
  \item the edge — \textquotedblleft{}Spanish and Portuguese kept theirs\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three languages made the same swap? (\textbf{French}, \textbf{German}, \textbf{Italian}.) Was it three separate inventions? (\textbf{No} — one change spreading by \textbf{contact} across a connected block.) What is that kind of change called? (\textbf{Areal}.) Which languages at the edge kept their simple past? (\textbf{Spanish} and \textbf{Portuguese}.) Next: everything together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — two pasts, and why}

\label{lesson:FR-C15-practice}



\begin{quote}
One tense to say and one to recognise. Run both, and keep the jobs separate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the one you say}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, tu as parlé, il a parlé, nous avons parlé, vous avez parlé, ils ont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}j'ai travaillé, nous avons habité\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three endings — \textquotedblleft{}é, i, u\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé, nous avons travaillé\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: the one you read}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pairs — \textquotedblleft{}il parla … il a parlé\textquotedblright{}; \textquotedblleft{}ils parlèrent … ils ont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sisters — \textquotedblleft{}il parla, habló, falou, parlò\textquotedblright{}
  \item the job — \textquotedblleft{}recognise it; do not say it\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the two histories}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item where the tense came from — \textquotedblleft{}I have letters, written ones\textquotedblright{}
  \item the fossil — \textquotedblleft{}Les lettres que j'ai écrites\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three retreats — \textquotedblleft{}passé simple, Präteritum, passato remoto\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{the past tense you will actually use}, built from \emph{avoir} and a participle that never moves.
  \item \textbf{three participle endings}, and the fact that one of them was spread by analogy rather than inherited.
  \item \textbf{an origin}: the tense began as plain possession and hardened, which is why it uses \emph{have} at all — and why a participle still agrees when its object comes first.
  \item \textbf{a second past you only read}, and the reason it is only read: not because the form is fancy, but because a block of neighbouring languages stopped saying theirs at roughly the same time, and the ones at the edge did not.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}they worked.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Ils ont travaillé}.) Which part of the compound past changes? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}}.) Which three forms of \emph{parler} are homophones? (\emph{\textbf{parler, parlé, parlez}}.) What is \emph{il parla}, and what do you do with it? (The \textbf{passé simple} — \textbf{recognise} it, never say it.) Why does the participle agree in \emph{les lettres que j'ai écrites}? (It was an \textbf{adjective} first, and the object comes \textbf{before} it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
